## Natural history notes

A small velvet ant characterized by its ant-like body, dense pale to reddish hairs, and wingless female form, while males are winged and more wasp-like. In Florida, it is part of the state’s velvet ant fauna and is likely encountered in sandy open habitats, pine flatwoods, scrub edges, trails, fields, and other areas where ground-nesting bees or wasps occur. It is not a true ant but a parasitoid wasp; females search on the ground for host nests and lay eggs on developing bee or wasp larvae, while adults may feed on nectar or other sugary resources and females can deliver a painful sting if handled.
